utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we start with the trial, maybe we could deal with a few housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we do that, I wonder if the witness could have his headphones placed on, just so he's not confused about what's going on while we deal with preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The day after tomorrow, on the 7th, there's going to be a swearing in of new Judges in the morning, which eats into our time in the morning. We are supposed to be sitting at 9.00, and the swearing in is going to take place at 9.00 to about 10.00. We are being asked to start our case at 10.00, and I hope that will be okay with everybody. Judge Hoepfel was showing me we were supposed to start at 10.30, but I was approached orally that 10.00 would be fine. We were being offered to sit until 3.00 in the afternoon or sometime around then. I don't think that will happen, because Judge Hoepfel and Judge Nosworthy are involved in another trial that afternoon starting at quarter to two or whatever -- quarter past two. So we will sit the normal time. We will break-up at the normal break time, but we will start at 10.00. Then on the 27th, again there is an almost unavoidable interruption. There is a meeting of the Judges starting at 9.00, which means that we will not be able to begin at 9.00 in the morning. However, we -- we will recall that we were given alternative dates or dates on which we could sit both morning and afternoon, and we have -- the Chamber has established that the afternoon of the 27th is still available. The question is: Is everybody amenable to sitting in the afternoon on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The Prosecution certainly is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is all right. But have I understood you correctly? Would the hearing be held in the afternoon on the 27th? Would the hearing be held in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry. I was on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid any errors as far as our schedule is concerned, the hearing wouldn't start at 10.00 or 11.00, it would start at 2.15 on the 27th. This would suit us, by all means, if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, that's the intention, sir; we start at 2.15 on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then those are the changes that will be effected. We will start at 2.15 on the 27th, and at 10.00 on Friday this week. Thank you so much. That's all from me insofar as housekeeping is concerned. I guess you are calling the next witness, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Luka Brkic, who is present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could Mr. Brkic please make the declaration. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has to inform the Chamber of the fact that ten or 15 minutes ago we received an addition to the witness's statement, the witness who will be giving evidence today. This addition is in English, and the accused is not familiar with the text. The witness gave his statement in the year 2000. That was six years ago, and now we're being provided with an addition to his statement which contains a series of extremely important additions that concern the conditions in the prison in Knin, in military or civil prison. So this is completely new, and we haven't been prepared for this. We prepared ourselves on the basis of the existing witness statement. The evidence we were going to use was also evidence that we decided to use in the light of the statement we had. This isn't the first time such a situation has occurred. We had the same situation with the witness Hamdija Krupic. But with the help of the Chamber and through the efforts we made, we managed to have the hearing on that day and to avoid any problems, to avoid requests for the postponing of hearing that witness, but this is a very serious matter. There are many facts that we haven't been able to verify, we haven't been able to speak to our client about them or to see the manner in which we would conduct our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be seated in the meantime. And you can take your seat in the meantime. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Milovancevic is correct. We did provide a supplementary information sheet at noon. In fact, I called them to tell them it was coming because, as counsel said, it included more detail about detention which was not included in the prior statements. I think I should explain to Your Honours how this happened. This witness was scheduled to arrive here on Monday for proofing, the ordinary proofing that we do, which oftentimes produces some supplementary information. His flight was cancelled because of weather, and so he just arrived yesterday afternoon. I completed the proofing today at 11.30, and by noon I had had a chance to type up the additional information and e-mailed it to Defence counsel, and certainly we -- we endeavour to disclose any new information as quickly as possible. They learned about this right after I did, but I recognise that it's much less notice than we usually like to give to Defence counsel for new information. As far as other cases go or other instances in this case, Your Honour, it is a practice at this Tribunal that you have a proofing session with a witness, additional information does often come out of that, and we disclose that to the Defence as quickly as we can. I guess I don't understand Defence counsel to be challenging that practice, it's been upheld in other cases, and we would submit that it helps the Defence counsel by avoiding surprises in the courtroom. The new information in the supplementary information sheet is limited to this issue of detention in Knin. It's information which I learned this morning, just a few hours ago. What we would propose, Your Honour, is we're certainly flexible to try to accommodate the Defence to allow them to study this overnight if they need to. They could start the cross-examination of this witness tomorrow. I think his evidence in chief will last a good part of today. They could certainly cross-examine on the rest of the information which goes to the attack on Skabrnja, it has nothing to do with the detention that came later. An alternate position would be we could allow them to cross-examine this witness on Friday and we could go ahead and call the next witness tomorrow. What we tried to do, Your Honour -- I realise this is an unusual circumstance, but we're trying to fill the court days as best we can. Some witnesses take less time, particularly on cross-examination, than we had anticipated, some take more, and with this particular witness, because his flight was cancelled due to weather, it just put us in a time crunch and that's why this information has come later than usual. But we would say the way to deal with that is just if the Defence needs until tomorrow before they can begin cross, or until Friday, then we will accommodate that in whatever way we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say. There's just one little point that I don't understand, Mr. Black; why, if this witness was proofed four, five, six years ago, suddenly new information comes up today. And not only with this witness but with any other witness. Why does it happen always -- almost always that suddenly new matter comes up which didn't come up in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's almost inevitable by the way that these -- these cases are investigated and tried. As you mention, his statement was taken in 2000 by investigators who no longer work at this Tribunal. I certainly didn't work at this Tribunal when the statement was taken, and so by the time the witness comes and we have a concrete case in which he's going to testify and we go through the process of finding out what he remembers from his statement, if there are any changes, if there are corrections, you inevitably get more detail on some issues, some things he doesn't remember. I'm afraid, Your Honour, that happens with almost every witness, and that's why -- part of why we have proofing in these supplemental information sheets, to provide that information to the Defence as soon as we find out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All I'm saying is more detail I can understand, but a new issue is what I don't understand. Obviously, when this witness was proofed in 2000, the war in the region was long over, so he should have been in a position to cover all areas that he wanted to testify on. It's not as if the detention in Knin took place after 2000, after he had given his statement. It took place before he gave that statement, and what I don't understand is why a whole area, a whole point, is left out. Not detail but a whole point that needs to be canvassed is left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be that as it may, I understand that you will not be able to resolve the issue or to answer me satisfactorily on that point and it's a point that I'm just raising as a concern from the Bench that it doesn't seem to be logical for a whole point to be forgotten and then to come up last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify for you. It's not an entirely new issue. His detention is mentioned in his statement. It's also addressed in slightly more detail in a 1992 statement to the Croatian police, which the Defence have. What we've obtained is more detail. He's clarified for me the places where he was detained, and he's talked to me about the conditions of detention, because I asked him about that today. It's not an entirely new issue, but I -- but I do recognise that the amount of detail is significant, but it's not a new issue, Your Honour. So I just want to assure you, I hope, on that point that it's not a brand new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milovancevic, there are suggestions by the Prosecution that you might perhaps want to delay your cross-examination on the Knin issue until tomorrow or until Friday. How -- how do you react to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we accept this suggestion in principle. We're doing our best to ensure that we find solutions to the problems that arrive to avoid additional expenses, to avoid postponing the proceedings. Since the witness is already here and expenses have already been incurred, let's start with the examination-in-chief today. And then as far as the cross-examination is concerned, when it comes to new details, I think we could commence with this part of the cross-examination tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. I think we'll have time to do that tomorrow. But the problem was the new material that we were provided with today. And there's something else I would like to add. I do not share the position of my colleague from the Prosecution when he says it's not a new theme. In the statement that we received from the year 2000 there is only one piece of information that concerns the accused who was in the prison mentioned. Now we're speaking about civilian prisons, the role of Martic, and a series of facts that -- a series of facts that are quite new to us and this is why we have reacted in this way. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. The Bench is grateful to you for your cooperation and it appreciates that. I believe you heard the Bench's concern to the Prosecution about statements that come late. The matter cannot be taken much further, and we shall then proceed and hope that you'll have enough time to prepare to cross-examine in those areas of the case that are new.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I also express my appreciation to Defence counsel for being flexible in their approach, and I would say that-- hopefully it goes without saying but I will say it anyhow, that we try to avoid this situation and we try to disclose new information as quickly as we can and we will continue to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to have kept you waiting a little bit while we've discussed some other matters. Can you please stand and read the declaration that's being handed to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkic. Can you understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You can scoot your chair forward, if it makes you more comfortable. If at any time you don't understand one of my questions, please just tell me and I'll try to ask it more clearly. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: My name is Luka Brkic. I am from Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what year were you born, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of October, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you attend elementary school in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: In Skabrnja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And later, I believe during 1976 and 1977, you went to nightschool in Zadar to become a truck driver; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I obtained my licence in Germany, but in Zadar I got my Yugoslav licence or, rather, my German one was recognised and I was delivered a Yugoslav licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you for clarifying that. Did you serve in the JNA at some point?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What year was that or what years?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you receive any specialised training in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I was just a member of the engineer unit. The pioneer engineers unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I'm going to ask you about your personal background. Now I'm going to begin asking you some questions about Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know you're all familiarity stage with Skabrnja, but I just remind you that it can be seen on page 30 of the atlas in grid A1. So at the upper left-hand side of page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, during 1991 was there a village guard in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: In which year? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In 1991, was there a village guard?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was some village guards, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When was that established, do you remember? What month?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was established in June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you yourself become a member of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was towards the end. Perhaps one month before Skabrnja was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very briefly, could you explain why the village guard in Skabrnja was established?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was part of the Territorial Defence, and that's how it worked. That's how the system functioned in every town and every village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, were you part of the Territorial Defence in 1991 or are you discussing the -- the system prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but only towards the end because I was in Sibenik working there. I couldn't be a permanent member, but I was part of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did this village guard that you were a member of, did they have uniforms in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you get uniforms at any point before you left Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the beginning of the conflict. Perhaps a month before the beginning of the conflict we received eastern -- we received uniforms from eastern Germany, uniforms that had already been used. I don't quite know when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the village guard part of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can explain that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say the village guard was part of the Territorial Defence, sir, can you give us a little bit more explanation, what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was at the level of local communes. At that point in time, they formed a reserve police force, and then after a short while the -- it was transformed into the village guards and to a defence system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you were telling us about the uniforms. Did everyone in the village guard receive a uniform?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, not everyone. Not at the beginning. Later on everyone received a uniform when the attack was about to commence. That was also the case with the weapons that were received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you receive?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: People had hunting rifles, shotguns. People received automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs. There were various kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you yourself have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the attack commenced, about five days before the attack commenced I was issued with a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. A couple more questions before I leave this topic. Was the village guard in Skabrnja, was that part of the Croatian army in any way?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: At the time, the army hadn't been formed. All that was in existence was the ZNG, the National Guard in Zagreb. Everything else was part of the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And were you and the other village guards in Skabrnja part of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, no. Only people who had gone to Zagreb were members of the ZNG, or people who had gone to other areas where the ZNG was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm going to turn and ask you some specific questions about events until November of 1991. What were you doing on the night of 17 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: On that night, I was on guard for a certain period of time. It was at night-time. I was on guard until about 3.00, and then a second group took over, the group that came to harm in the attack itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where did you go when you finished your guard shift?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I went home to rest. And all the boys who were with me did so too. There were seven of us in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm going to turn the 18th of November, 1991, and I want you to take this step-by-step and focus on what happened to you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What's the first thing you remember seeing or hearing on the morning of 18 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I was still in bed at the time. Behind the house I was in, that's the house behind my brother's house, well, the first shell fell on a plain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what did you do when you heard that shell fall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, if I can interrupt -- translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is an SOS coming from that cubicle there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The English booth was on the Albanian channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The English booth has now gone back to its place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Brkic. We had a technical problem with the interpretation. Could you tell us what you did when you heard the first shelling falling in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I jumped out of my bed, and I had slept in the uniform, the one from East Germany that I had. We wore parts of uniform and parts of civilian clothes. Actually, we slept in our street clothes at the time. Anyway, I was dressed when I jumped up from bed, and I told my wife something is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the clothes, what precisely were you wearing when you jumped out of bed? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had my jeans on. The trainers were next to the wall, next to the coat-tree. I had a windbreaker with a hood when I went hunting or into the field on an inspection tour. That's what I managed to put on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you put on any other part of the uniforms that you'd received from East Germany or from ...

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. All I managed to grab was a rucksack and a helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do next? Did you go outside your house or did you stay inside?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I went outside, and in that short time five or six boys managed to gather, and they had all come to me asking me what to do. Since the tanks were already not more than 15 minutes -- 15 metres away, there was a little transformer station also in the vicinity, I advised them to run away, to find shelter somewhere beyond the houses, beyond the road, along walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: These five or six boys that you mentioned, who were they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were also people who normally shared the night guard, night village guard with me who were not on duty at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you said you advised them to run away. Did you tell them where they should go?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told them to go beyond the houses that are beyond the road, because I was with my house on this side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did those -- those boys or those men, did they follow your advice and leave?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did as I said, and that's what saved their skins. I told them, "If you find yourself in danger, there's nothing you can do but run towards the village and just look out for yourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when they left, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I went to my brother's house. I went to the attic to see if some boys still remained there or they had already gone downstairs. At that time, the second shell hit. It hit the centre of the roof beam. And since it was a small mortar shell, I can't tell you the exact calibre, but it didn't fall further down into the house. It was sort of -- it short of ricochetted from the roof beam.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now you've mentioned the first shell and the second shell. Were those the only shells falling --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were those -- were those --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: That's all that hit us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about in other parts of the village? Could you hear or see if there were shells falling on other parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: When the shooting started, that was the start of the conflict. The howitzers came in, the aeroplanes, and all the village was under attack. And there is a map that comes from their side, and they drew the map, not I. It shows from where fire was opened. It shows the strength of their weapons, which howitzers, which calibres, from which positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we should have a chance to look at that map a little later, but let me focus now on your story and what happened to you. What did you do when this second shell hit your brother's house that you were in?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I left the attic. There were two other people with me, Marin and a man nicknamed Neno. His name was actually Ante.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What's the surname of Marin and Neno?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Gurlica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where did you and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are they both Gurlica?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, are they both named Gurlica?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's both their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you and Marin and Neno go when you left the attic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were not in the attic. They were around the house. I was the only one up in the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, explain that to me. Tell me what happened when you came down from the attic. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I checked around the house, because that's where the combat armoured vehicle did most of its shooting, in a pinewood, from a pinewood near the house, and there was a lot of brush burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when -- and when you went to check around the house, is that when you saw Marin and Neno?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. When I saw that I couldn't find them, I realised they must have found cover somewhere. So I went down to the basement where women and children were sheltering. I realised there was nothing much I could do upstairs, so I went to join them downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. In which house is this basement in that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: My brother's house. It was just next door to my house. We share the same yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And who was in the basement? Do you remember any specific names of who was there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I remember all the names. There was my wife, my mother, the Gurlica women, Neno's mother, grandmother, the children. There was another neighbour also name Gurlica. Practically the extended Gurlica family. There was also an infirm man, Ivan Gurlica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how old these people were, the people who were in the basement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: There was only one old man, this Ivan Gurlica. All the other men were around 40, or there were young boys who had just done their military service, like Marin and Neno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about the women who were in the cellar? Do you remember approximately ages?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were either the age of my mother, in their 60s, or around the age of my wife, 40-ish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And other than -- than yourself, was anyone else in the basement a member of the Skabrnja village guard?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Only Marin and Neno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And were there any weapons in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was one light machine-gun, two automatic rifles, one Kalashnikov, and one from the former Yugoslav People's Army, a folding one -- no, not a folding one. The normal one. 50 something. I don't know the number. And there was one shotgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Black. The witness has said that in fact the only other persons in the basement were members of the Skabrnja village guard were Neno and Marin, but as far as I understood from the previous evidence, those persons were still outside. He thought they had got cover. They're not supposed to be in the basement. Or have I missed something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Let me -- I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you've her the Judge's remark. When did Neno and Marin come to be in the basement with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Right. I forgot to say that. They joined us later. The lady is quite right to remark this. Once I got into the basement, and I said that in my statement, somebody started to knock on the door. I didn't know it was them, and I thought it could be that army that had come, but it wasn't. They were trying to get me to open the door because it was locked, and I did. I let them into the basement. And just seconds after that the balcony door was broken and the troops started rushing in, the paramilitaries, or I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to that, just a couple more questions about Neno and Marin. Do you remember what they were wearing when they came to the basement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Neno and Marin were wearing camouflage uniforms, and I managed to persuade both of them to take it off. Neno just didn't have enough time to get off -- to take his boots off, because I had told them, "If they find you like this, you will be liquidated immediately." Underneath the uniforms one of them had a tracksuit on and the other one was in jeans, like I, and a T-shirt, and that's the way we were dressed, one in a tracksuit and two of us in jeans and T-shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I interrupted you just when you said you heard the balcony door being opened. Tell us what happened then.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. No. They didn't open doors. They didn't even try. They just shattered the glass on the windows and broke in. The basement did not have stairs leading to the basement. There was just a -- an aluminum ladder as a makeshift solution, and they shouted from above the ladder, "Get out or we are throwing a grenade in." So I told Neno that I would do it, because he was a young boy and he was afraid. It was a nicely done basement. It was a good shelter. You can't easily throw a grenade in. So I went out. The man -- the soldier asked me to lift the ladder. I did, and there was no more shooting for a while. And first the old women and children came out and then all the rest of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened once everyone had come out of the basement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They made us lie down outside the house on the concrete with our arms outstretched until this Captain Jankovic ordered us to stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Who was it who made you lie down?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Those who came first. They were all wearing camouflage uniforms and had their faces painted. We couldn't recognise anybody except for one man whom I knew from working in the Jadran quarry. He searched me, and he found in my pocket a length of cord, the kind that you use to clean a rifle, and there were two cases -- casings from a shotgun, and he asked me, "What is this?" And I said, "I don't know. I don't know where I got it from." There was a tall man with black hair behind him. He twisted my neck from behind and made a motion as if to slit my throat, but I said, "Oh, don't do that. Don't slit my throat for nothing." And at that moment Captain Jankovic showed up and told him to stop. And then this same Captain Jankovic told us to get up and go to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you and just ask you a few questions about what you've told us. First you describe the soldier as wearing camouflage uniforms. Did you notice if they had any kind of insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. At the point when women had already left, I was standing next to the first tank, next to Captain Jankovic, and on my right there were soldiers with the insignia of White Eagles, and one of them asked me, "Do you know what this means?" I didn't dare to say a word. I was too afraid. And he said, "These are the White Eagles." I kept silent. And they belonged to the regular troops, but most of them were in fact reservists. I could see it from their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say the regular troops or reservists, to what armed force are you referring there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I meant to say that it was the regular army made up of conscripts who were doing their military service, whereas reservists were people who had been conscripted for the wartime effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but the question, Witness, is, are these reservists or conscripted people in the army of Yugoslavia, in the army of Russia, in the army of England? Which army did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reservists belonged to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what about the people you call the regular troops? Did they also belong to the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were also members of the Yugoslav army. Maybe I didn't put it too clearly, but that's what I men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's okay. We understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By Yugoslav army, what do you mean? The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what existed until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you mean that they're a part of the JNA? Is that who you're referring to, or are you referring to another group?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I meant the JNA. And they were conscripted formally into the JNA, although they did not act under the JNA's standard. They acted the way they acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we're clear on that now. You mentioned some insignia of the White Eagles. Did you notice any other kind of insignia besides the White Eagles and these regular JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. They were still wearing the five-pointed star. Some officers that I saw at the outskirts of the village wore ceremonial uniforms in part, and others wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I think maybe you misunderstood my question. I wasn't asking about the different kinds of JNA uniforms but if you saw any other kinds of insignia besides White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Some wore emblems of SAO Krajina. Some wore cockades, the hats that were worn in the first -- in the Second World War, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Before I interrupted you to ask you these questions about uniforms, you were explaining how one of the witnesses was threatening you and someone named Jankovic intervened. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's correct. They wanted to drag me away behind a house to kill me. However, one man said, "I know this guy. He is a Siptar." He just said that. I don't know why, because he didn't really know me. He just wanted to save me. Then Captain Jankovic got this man to release me, the man who was twisting my neck from the back, and he sort of made a motion that he would shoot them if they don't leave me alone. And he said, "This is no army. I thought that there were Chetniks here, but this is just a gang, riff-raff." From all I saw, from the impression this Captain Jankovic made, I think he was the only soldier there. All the others were picked from the surrounding villages, and they did their looting and destroying without Jankovic's knowledge. They were doing it behind his back. And they had to be reservists. Who else could they have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that Jankovic was the only soldier there, but yet you said that you think the others were reservists, did you think that the other people were there in a private capacity, or were they there as some sort of armed force? It's not quite clear to me what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were together with Jankovic, and they were within the army, but they were actually doing what they were doing without Jankovic's knowledge and quite apart from any army activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. One thing just -- just so the record's clear. You said that someone referred to you as a Siptar. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: To facilitate my liquidation. That's the only thing that could have meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But Siptar, is there another word for that, what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Siptar is what we call people from Kosovo, Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Brkic, you explained to us how Captain Jankovic intervened on your behalf and then -- and then he told you to get up and go to the road. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant. He didn't let them shoot me. What I just described happened when I came to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And after that incident that you've just described, what happened next? Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I put my hands behind my head, and I followed him all day until dusk, until we reached the church, I and all the other captives who were following him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I'm clear on this. The other people who were in the basement with you, were all those people still with you when you walked to the church or when you went to the church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: There was late Petar, Marin. They were with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What about the women and children who had been in the basement? Were they still with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The women and children, as I said before, had been separated from us, and they went towards the outskirts of the village, towards the road, towards a place called Ambar. We actually live on the outskirts, on the periphery of Ambar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you and Petar and Marin followed Captain Jankovic towards the church. Can you describe how you went there? Describe that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It's easy to describe that. You stopped above Petrova -- Petrova's house very briefly. A tank stopped there and they opened fire there. A Zolja was used to fire on a house. Somebody fired from a Zolja to make sure nobody was hiding inside. At the same time a tank opened fire in the direction of the school. It fired one shell. Another shell was fired from behind on the houses to the left of the school, but I think they were before the school. I haven't mentioned this anywhere, they were engaged in shelling constantly. They didn't just fire one shell. The road was full of shells. I didn't want to mention each and every shell or -- that was fired, or each and every explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain what a Zolja is?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It's a sort of hand-held rocket launcher. It's intended for single use. Once you use it you discard it. Whereas a hand-held launcher is something you can use on numerous occasions. That's the sort of weapon I had in the former army so I'm quite familiar with this sort of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned some -- you mentioned tanks and you said that you were also going with a couple others. Were you together with the tanks or were they ahead of you or behind you? Where were the tanks in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We were to the left of the road. We were at an equal distance as the captain from the tank, and there were three others who followed me. I didn't dare turn around, because if you turned around, well, you know what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You said you were an equal distance as the captain from the tank. Can you give an idea how far that distance was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a step or two away from the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's a convenient time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, actually my math is -- I'm thinking of the morning session. Do we have another 15 minutes? The court officer tells me we do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Brkic, just thinking about the next break which will be in 15 minutes. Other than Captain Jankovic, did you recognise any of the other people either in the tanks or who were with the tanks as you moved towards the church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. I didn't recognise anyone now. I couldn't have known them. I couldn't have recognised them since they were all masked. Then we stopped bit church itself. I assume there was someone there who had worked with me for five days, but I can't say that for sure. He was wearing a cap. When he got off the tank, he tapped me on the shoulder. He probably knew me. And he said, "Nothing will happen to you." That was someone who was in the first tank, and the event I'm describing is something that occurred when he came out of the tank, got down from the turret.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember what he was wearing, what kind of uniform or what kind of clothes he had on?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: He was wearing the sort of uniform a tank crew wears. He had a cap with protection for his ears. He had the sort of things that soldier would wear on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, with the assistance of the court officer and the usher, if we could show Exhibit 271, please. And in particular, it's the page with the ERN 04687818. Mr. Brkic, in a moment on the screen in front of you there will be a photograph, so when it comes up I just want you to look at it, please. Mr. Brkic, do you recognise the building in the photograph there on the left?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the village church or the local church. Call it as you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the same church that you've just mentioned or is that a different one?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No, that's the church I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And where within the village of Skabrnja is this church located?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We say that the church is in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure we need to see the image any more. Well, maybe we can leave it up in case it helps the witness. Mr. Brkic, did anything happen to this church on that day that you saw?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened to the church on that day. Shells were fired, mortar shells were fired. And then later on when we arrived, when the tank stopped, what we can see in this photograph is -- well, you have a path here that you can see. Perhaps you can go back to the previous photograph. If you stop there, I'm pointing to the location of one tank with this pointer, and there was another tank here. They tried to go to the church, to enter the church. This was done wilfully, without Captain Jankovic having provided authorisation. He said that the rubble would fall on him. He then returned to the same position, and several soldiers then entered the church, and they attacked the altar, the icons, everything that was in the church. They broke things up. They fired shots. I didn't see this, but these are things that I could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. One thing, you said they tried to enter the church. How did -- how did they try to enter the church at first?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: You can see that in the photograph. You have some stairs here, and then someone gave -- gave up this idea. Perhaps he realised he couldn't enter the church. Perhaps they realised the tank couldn't enter the church. This was perhaps just a provocative act.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. It's just not particularly clear, but you say perhaps they realised the tank couldn't enter the church. Was someone trying to enter the church with a tank? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the tank, with the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining that to me. While you were here near the church as you've just described, at some point did those Serb soldiers come under fire? Do you remember that, something like that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as the tank we've just been discussing, I remember that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the last question the Prosecutor was talking about Serbian soldiers. The witness has never used such an expression so far. He mentioned reservists, JNA soldiers, but the term used by the Prosecutor is not one used by the witness, so it is quite incorrect to quote him in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to clarify with the witness. The phrase I used was "Serb" as opposed to "Serbian."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you know the -- could you tell the ethnicity of any of these soldiers that you saw on that day in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to say what their ethnicity was. Some boys escorted me, and then later on there were boys from Zagreb who were serving in the military. There were youths, boys who had come from Zadar at the time. They came to testify. There was some sportsmen in Skabrnja too. They didn't even know that Skabrnja was being attacked. They thought it was some sort of an exercise. That's how it had been portrayed to them. So the person who took me back to a certain place said he would never return again. He said, "I'll never return here." He says, "I'm doing my military service." He said, "I've come down from Zagreb." There were young men there who were unaware of the fact that the village was to be attacked. They thought it was some sort of a routine training.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that some of the people that participated in the attack were Croatians? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. One of them was. He testified in Zadar. There were such cases too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So other than these people you've mentioned from Croatia or Zagreb or Zadar, could you tell if there were people there who were not Croats?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: At the time, I couldn't distinguish between Serbs or Croats. Some had the five-pointed star on them. Until I arrived in Knin, and then I saw that the insignia that the soldiers had consisted of the letters J and

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They no longer had the five-pointed star as insignia. All they had were the letters J and A, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's not get to Knin yet. I still want to talk to you what happened in Skabrnja on the 18th of November. Do you know what ethnicity captain -- do you know what ethnicity Captain Jankovic is -- was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say. They called him Lala. His men called him Lala, and when he didn't allow the church to be shelled, he told me, "Why should sacred or holy buildings or schools be destroyed -- or schools? Why should they be destroyed?" He said, "I'm also interested in those holy buildings." Later I heard that his wife was either from Zadar or someone in fact told me that she had worked with him, and no one wanted to say who this one was. I think his wife was a Croat. And this is why I think that in part he was interested in these holy buildings. He was tied to these holy buildings such as the church in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you think that Jankovic's wife was a Croat. Do you have any idea what ethnicity he was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I think he was probably from Vojvodina. He was someone from Vojvodina. As to whether he was a Croat or a Hungarian or whether he was some other ethnicity perhaps, a Slovakian, I really couldn't say. They called him Lala. Whether that was his nom de guerre or whether that was his real name I couldn't say that either. In all wars, and that was probably the case in this war too, people would use pseudonyms to conceal their identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. One more question on this and then I'll move away from this. So you mentioned one person whom you know at least from Croatia. Was that a person Croatian by ethnicity the person that you know that participated in this attack?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know any Croats. I only knew this young man who drove me in the vehicle. He was doing his military service. He was a member of the regular military. I don't know if you understand what this term means exactly, but I identified him as a Croat and he told me he was a Croat. But as for the others, I didn't know what their nationality was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that was my question. Do you tell the nationality of anyone else who participated in the attack on Skabrnja, other than that one person?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Before we got onto this topic, you were telling me about when -- an occasion when the soldiers there came under fire. Can you please tell me what happened?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I think I was talking about the tank when we stopped in front of the church. And beyond the fields there's a village, a hamlet, called Gravici. Two or three shots were fired, probably sniper shots, and there, by the tank, was Captain Dragan… or Zoran. He went to the other side of the tank, and I was used as a sort of live shield. I was standing there when they opened fire, and the captain later went behind the tank. He took me behind a house the house that was on the corner there and he said, "Flee from here. You'll be killed by your own people." Then one person who wanted to kill a young boy called Marin, he said, "I saw where they were firing from, and he pointed in the direction in the direction they were firing from. And then he turned the tank around, opened fire, and missed the house. The shell fell by the house. He then fired a second shell and said, "This time I won't miss." And that was, in fact, what happened. He didn't miss. When I came from the prison, I went to see how the shell had shot -- had been fired and had hit the house. It had hit the house at the top of the steps to the house. That's what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is now time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We will take a short break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, we're going to start asking you some questions again, but I'm going to ask you to make an effort to speak slowly and to really listen to my questions, because the interpreters are having trouble interpreting everything that you're saying. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I know you have a lot of information which you want to share, but please make an effort not to talk over me while I'm talking, while I'm still asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Before the break, you'd said how you -- you talked about Captain Jankovic and the things that he had done to help you. Was Captain Jankovic present when they tried to drive the tank into the church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was present, but he wasn't right by the tank itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Was he able to see what was happening to the church? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he could see what was happening to the church just as I could because he was quite close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just before we broke, you said, "Then one person who wanted to kill a young boy called Marin," and he said something, but I'd like you to explain this incident where someone wanted to kill Marin.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: He tried to till the young child, and a nurse was present. There were the three of them. Nada Pupovac was closest to him, and she was in fact the person who gave orders to all of them. She said, "Don't kill him. We've had enough of such things." She was referring to what had happened there at the beginning. And he gave up on this idea of killing him, and that's how this matter ended. We mentioned this shooting, and he said that he had seen where the tank had fired from. He did what he did. He opened fire from the tank. One of the shells missed the target, the other shell hit the target, and that's all I wanted to say, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. And you explained that to us before the break but just a few more questions about this incident with Marin. Where did that happen? Where was it that this person wanted to kill Marin?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: This happened behind the house of the corner where the captain took shelter and later on everyone else took shelter there after the three shots had been fired, the three shots that were fired at the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And who was it -- who was the person who -- who wanted to kill Marin?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. He was in camouflage uniform. It was probably the person, the tall person who wanted to kill me, too, who wanted to cut my throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that further detail. While you were in the area of the church, did you see any other officers besides Captain Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as the officers are concerned, I think Calic was there. He was at the entrance. He had a desk and a chair, and he gave orders to Captain Jankovic and to everyone else who opened fire along that road to the village and in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. For the time being I'm just focused on the time where you were near the church. Did you see this Calic or any other officers there near the church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: A lorry was sent, a TAM 110, to fetch him, to fetch that officer. And this is what happened. And once the officers had been fetched, he said, "Well, look." That's how everything ended. And he said, "That's how I would issue orders too." That was a sort of joke of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when you say "this officer," are you referring to Calic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I think Calic was an officer, but there were several of them who were involved in coordinating the attack. Calic was there on one side. There were others elsewhere, but I think he's the one, because I know for sure that he gave orders to issue -- to open fire. He issued orders to open fire. I know Calic is an officer, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me focus just on what you saw. Did you see this officer Calic or any other officers in the area of the church? You yourself, did you see them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I personally saw someone. He wasn't there before. He was fetched to come to the place where we were, to the place where the captain and the tank were. But what should be said and hasn't been said is that they reported that Vukovar had fallen, and then they reported that Skabrnja had fallen too. This was reported over the radio. A sold year had a radio set. They were happy about this. They celebrated this a bit. There was a shop nearby. They got some drinks. They had a few drinks and had some fun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that it's perfectly clear, who do you mean by "they," that they reported that Vukovar had fallen and that they were happy about this. Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They heard this on the radio. As to whether this came directly from Vukovar or somewhere else, I don't know, but this person who had a radio set received the information. He told all of them that Vukovar had fallen. This was at the same time that they arrived in our place, in Skabrnja, when Skabrnja fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Please just listen to my question carefully. Who is "they"? Are you referring to the soldiers or some other people? Who is it that you're referring to as "they"?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the soldiers who were on the other side either in Vukovar, and that's where they received that information. They received that information, and the people concerned are the troops, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. The troops, the soldiers. They were with you near the church in Skabrnja. Are those the people you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the people I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on a little bit in your story. Did you eventually leave the church or the area of the church?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was then time for Calic to leave, if it was Calic. We followed him in another vehicle. We headed towards the entrance to the village of Ambar. We went along the main road. We were placed in the cellar of two houses that had been abandoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that cellar at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, we stayed in the cellar for a little over an hour perhaps, maybe even two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who else was there at the entrance to the village besides you among the villagers of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Some women had been put up there. Some had already set off for Benkovac. Later I heard they were in the nursery school, that the women were staying in the nursery school. And then as mother and grandmother and other Gurlicas were there, and an Eva Segaric. A Lejla Segaric. There were about ten of us in that cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was anybody mistreated when you were at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: There was Neno, a soldier who cleaned weapons for -- with night vision, took him behind the house, beat him up a bit and then returned him. His mother was trying. I thought that he was going to kill him since he had a weapon in his hands, but he didn't kill him. He sent him back to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us you stayed in the cellar for a little over an hour, maybe two hours. What happened next? Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They then took us out. I took Ella with me she was poor sighted she could see but not very well because it was night. There was a bus parked there and they then took us to the bus. We stood by the bus. Neno Marin and myself were lined up there by the edge of the road. They ordered us to line up. I thought they were going to execute us. We lined up. We were facing them, and they said, "We don't want you Ustashas to watch us killing you. Turn around." I then thought they were really going to kill us, but they then cocked their rifles but they didn't open fire. Perhaps they were trying to scare us. And then they suddenly ordered us to turn and face them. In fact, before that they said, "We're not going to kill you immediately. Kick them in the legs so the Ustasha can feel what pain is." They were using provocative language. And then afterwards we had to turn to face them. Once we had done that, they order us to head to the buses, and as we were getting into the buses they beat us. We then got into the bus. I sat on the rear seat. I sat behind the seat. I hoped that that would prevent them from beating me too severely. But while we were in the buses they didn't beat us. And that is how we arrived in Benkovac. When we arrived in Benkovac, someone called Reks whom I have heard of but I've never seen him there was some sort of celebration and singing at Oscar's. This person was wearing some sort of a coat at an entrance at the reception. When will we got out of the bus he appeared. He appear. He almost trampled over me. When we arrived in a room he this put us all in that room where we had to sit down on the floor. They put our legs against the walls which were blood spattered. I don't know if someone had been there before we arrived but they were blood spattered -- blood splattered. Some people were at the windows. They provoked us, called us Ustashas. Others beat us. Then someone called Stevo Pupovac we worked together, I had worked with his sons. One approached me from behind but I'd already been beaten up by the others, and he was then going to pull me back and break my spine by digging his knees into my back. He jumped on me. He hit me. I turned around and I recognised his brother. When I turned around he recognised me and he said, "Sorry I didn't know it was you." Which means if it had been somebody else, he would have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. How long did you stay in this -- this place in Benkovac that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We slept on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in a moment I'm going to move on and ask you questions about the next day, but I have just a couple of short topics before I get there, okay? Do you know if any civilians were killed in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. I had already seen the corpses lying by the road. The soldier who was escorting us, whom I already told you was a Croat from somewhere around Zagreb, pulled us away so that we wouldn't look. I heard other people say that there was some women's corpses lying by the road, but I saw only one body with my own eyes. So there had been victims already then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you recognise the person that you saw with your own eyes? Do you know that person's name?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't. The body was lying away from me, facing away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you later learn about any particular people that were killed that day? Do you remember any names that you later learned of people who died?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later, I learned a lot of things, but it was much later. That day I had no way of knowing because I ended up in Benkovac, in the barracks. Only in Knin did I hear about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me. Now with the assistance of the court officer and the usher, I'm going to show you a map, and it has the ERN 04693957.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the easiest thing would be if this could be pulled up on e-court and at the same time we can give the a witness hard copy because I think it will be easier for him to deal with the hard copy. If the usher could please give him a copy. And in fact, we have copies -- I hope we have enough. We can give one to the Defence and one to each of Your Honours, if you like, just for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you recognise that map that's just to your left?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you provide this map to me yesterday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How did you obtain this map?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: After the Operation Storm, it was found in a place that housed the police administration. Not only this one but a lot of other documents. It was given to me, and I brought it here. It shows exactly the course of the attack. It's their army that drew this map, not I. It indicates all their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In just a moment I'll ask you to look at that, but who was it that gave it to you, this map?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The people who were involved in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember their names, or do you not remember their names?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was a neighbour of mine who gave it to me. He knew the man who participated in the operation. I don't know the man who actually took it from that police building. I know the man who gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at the map for a moment. Could you just look to your left, and maybe you can be provided with a pointer that will help you indicate things if you need to, and I want you just to very briefly explain to us the markings that are on this map. And I'll -- what I'd like you to do is, you know, go slowly but just point at one thing and then -- and then tell us what that is. Go slowly so that the interpreters and the rest of us can keep up with you, please. You have to do it to your left. There you go.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: This map depicts an operation that was called Alan. You see the signs denoting tanks or maybe little flags here Gornje Biljane that was designated as a command post as far as I know. Another command post was in a hamlet called Trljuge. November was in the house of a woman who moved to Germany. It was another house that held the headquarters. This here depicts the positions. And on the left side you see the time of the attack and where the attack started from. The tanks were parked there even earlier, in advance. I saw that because I had to see a man who lived --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. What time does it -- does it indicate the attack started?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It says here at Oscar 0600 hours, which means they started at 6.00. And fire was first opened at Skabrnja from the direction of Gornji Zemunik at 7.30. This is officially recorded here and people in the village remember it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this what you remember? Is that consistent with the times that you remember?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. All this is correct. It's consistent with the time that I remember. You see, this here, it says "105-millimetres." It's a battery of calibre 105. It's their gunnery positions. This is their airfield. They had fire support there, 122-millimetre cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But what does it -- there's a little diamond and a little circle and it tells what those stand for. What do those stand for according to this map?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: That denotes a tank, the diamond sign. And the other thing is a BOV, which is a combat armoured vehicle equipped with a heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you yourself see tanks and/or BOVs in Skabrnja on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a young blonde man in that vehicle. He was sight-setter. He was so young he looked more like a child and a soldier. He was the closest to me. There were two tanks, and he was between them. He was in this slot in the vehicle where ammunition is stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned specifically tanks. Did you also see any BOVs on that day?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to explain. That was the combat armoured vehicle quite close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand. Is there anything else on this map that you'd like to point out to us what it means?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The most active was this gun from is a Zapuzane, 120-millimetres. That was a position in Zapuzane from which they opened fire with these 120-millimetre cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just received this and we will seek a translation in due time but I would ask that it be given a number and admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an objection, Your Honour, on two grounds. First, the witness is speaking to this map, whatever it means, without being a military expert. The Prosecutor has already called their military expert and did not ask him anything about it. Second, we have to raise the question of authenticity of this map. The witness tells us that it's the plan of attack on Skabrnja. Maybe, maybe not. The proceedings will show. I just want to point out for the time being some details you can see on the monitor. The entire text in the margins on the map contains text in ball-point pen and then top right-hand corner, for instance, there is something overwritten in felt-tip pen. Then in the bottom right corner you have 120 millimetres. The 120 is in felt-tip pen, the rest the underlying text, is in ball-point pen. Then at the bottom of the page we see some sort of scale. All that is written on the map is in some way highlighted, overwritten, emphasised. We don't know who did it and why. The witness tells us he received this map from a person he knows, and that person received it from yet a third person who took it from a police station, some unknown police station. And third, this witness who is testifying to events of 15 years ago is producing documents. We had witness Segaric yesterday who produced some photographs, and now we have this witness producing a map. For all these reasons, I believe it will be difficult to accept this as -- as an authentic document at its face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the first point, I certainly don't think there's any requirement that a witness be a military expert to admit a map through him. It's true that our military expert testified earlier at which time we didn't have this map so there's no cans we could have asked him about it but I don't think it's necessary that he be an expert in order to tell what he was told about this map. As to the issue of authenticity, the Defence is entitled to make the points as they've done but we submit that goes to weight. Authenticity is not a requirement for admissibility under the rules. This witness has told where he got the document. He's told us that. And more importantly, he's told us some of the information on this document is consistent with his own experiences that he himself was present on the day of this attack. So we think that's a sufficient basis and certainly, Your Honour -- Your Honours will consider these issues when you decide what weight to give to this map, but we don't think that that goes -- that affects its admissibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just add to what I've already pointed out, Your Honour. The map is not dated. It's not signed, it's not sealed. There is no reference number. No indication of who it belongs to and who developed this map. I have nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me raise the first point, Mr. Milovancevic, that maybe in the future if you have an objection to any document being admitted into evidence, please rise before it is admitted. Don't rise after it has been admitted. That's the first point. You know, you are entitled at any stage to jump and object if there is something objectionable happening. Okay. Certainly speaking for myself, I don't know about the rest of the Bench, I -- I have the same questions that you had, Mr. Milovancevic, with respect to the map which I wanted to raise with the witness when the turn comes for the Bench comes to ask questions. But certainly, I don't know -- I find the rules of this Tribunal rather lax on the question of the admission of documents into evidence, and I think we had this problem at the beginning of the trial when we actually agreed that in a situation like this a document would then be marked for identification, and it could be looked at later. I don't know whether that kind of procedure would satisfy you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If I may just explain briefly. This map and the supplement to the witness's statement is something that we received just 15 minutes before today's hearing. That's why we were unable to react earlier. We are doing it now that it is in front of us. I hope you will acknowledge that. We were pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are missing the point. The point is, Mr. Black rose -- or he was on his feet and asked that -- after he had asked questions, he asked that this map be admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number, and you were sitting there and I kept quiet for a couple of seconds to give you an opportunity to stand if you were going to stand.
