Just when I finished admitting it you then rose. That's the point I'm referring to. I appreciate that you saw this map for the first time today with other documents, but when -- precisely because of that you should have been alert to rise before it was admitted or even before questions were asked about it. But be that as it may, my question to you is: Would marking it for identification be a satisfactory procedure at this stage? Because this is what is the guideline we agreed on at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, we will lift that admission of the document in evidence. We will mark it for identification and give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will marked for identification number 285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I just make an inquiry? If something is marked for identification, does that mean that Your Honours will place no weight on it or -- my concern is -- I recognise that there are questions that can be put to this witness by Your Honours or by me, I can follow up more, to try to establish as much as he knows about it, and therefore I think it should be admitted into evidence and then the weight can be decided by the Trial Chamber later. But I don't want to see it admitted -- marked for identification and not admitted and then at the end of the case we be in a position where we're not entitled to rely on this document at all. So I just want to clarify the status of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You queried the Chamber. You have been here much longer. What happens to documents marked for identification in terms of the procedure of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, my experience is limited to one other trial but documents that were simply marked for identification were not part of the record. They're simply marked for the convenience of the parties and the Court but they're not actually part of the Trial Record and therefore could not be relied upon in the judgement. And for that reason, I'm sorry to insist, but I would ask that it be admitted with its weight to be determined later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you're telling us you've got only one experience of this. The guideline that we all agreed on at the beginning was that where there was a dispute the document would be marked for identification, and the Trial Chamber will -- will look at the document and the evidence surrounding it when it deals with the weight of the evidence and decide on the basis of that information whether to admit it and give it any weight. Perhaps I'm not even right to say -- to decide whether to admit it, because I don't think that is part of the guideline. But I think the document will be treated in terms of the guideline that we outlined at the beginning, which was that it must be marked for identification in the case of a dispute like this, and the Trial Chamber will look at its weight when it looks at the totality of the evidence, and so it's ruled. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't feel like I should press this any further on the basis of what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. The ruling has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was that based on the standards governing the admission of evidence guidelines that Your Honours issued at the beginning of the trial? Is that what I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because at paragraph 6 it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you asking we reopen the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I -- I'm sorry, I just want to have clarity on this issue. It's respectfully done but I just want to follow what Your Honours have written here to make there's no confusion at the end of the case. I'll silt down if I am ordered to do so obviously but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are ordered to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I continue with the examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic now we're going to move to a new topic in your testimony. I want to ask you about the day after the attack on Skabrnja. What happened on the morning of 19 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, this map that is being contested now is just as I said in my statement before. Those three tanks that you see in depth in the background, that's what I saw. It's no forgery, as they seem to be saying. I can vouch that this is true. The map was brought as it was found. Nobody has any interest in forging such a map. Plus there are eyewitnesses to the entire operation. All these bunkers still exist today. The whole thing can be reconstructed if anybody wants to. There's no lying here. I don't see what anybody could gain about lying about this. This truly, faithfully reflects the positions as they were. Maybe some battery or position was not active for a while during this operation but that doesn't matter so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, let the Chamber remind you that you are not prosecuting the case. You are a witness. It is not for you to comment on the status of documents that are admitted. You answer the questions of the Prosecutor or whoever asks you questions, and you leave the process and the procedure of running the trial to the Chamber. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, let's just move now to the next day and tell me what happened on the morning of 19 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Only the 19th of November, in the morning, I wasn't there by that time. I was in Knin. In fact, in Benkovac in the morning, and by at that same evening in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's my question to you. In Benkovac on the morning of the 19th of November, what happened to you there in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: There were people whom I knew there. One nicknamed Arso, some work colleagues whom I used to see at the railway station, taxi drivers and forwarders, and they were looking for people who would go to Skabrnja, volunteers. They were looking for volunteers already in the morning. They were looking for people like me. And this Jarcov said with a sort of pride that Skabrnja doesn't exist any more and Nadin will go down the same path.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Where did you go? Did you leave Benkovac that morning?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, after they had had breakfast, they took us to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did anything happen on the way to Knin?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: On the way to Knin, they put us on the lorry, and then they would beat us. They had taken a guitar with them, and one of them played the guitar and sang some sort of songs to provoke us. If you moved or leaned against each other then they would hit you, beat you on your shoulders, on your back. So they mocked us. They stopped in Kistanje very briefly to display us as Ustashas. I have already underline the fact that we didn't have any uniforms, any Ustasha uniforms on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And who was it who was beating you and who was mocking you? Who? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The people escorting us. Well, they were the two sons of Stevo Pupovac who is also a transport worker. There was a doctor who lived in Skabrnja as a child that's not mentioned here, and he was there and some other people I did not know. There were four of them. One of the persons escorting us was someone I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How were these people dressed that were escorting you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. Like all other soldiers they were equipped. They said weapons and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know which force they were a part of?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they had already done their military service. They were a part of the reserve force. As to which army they were in, as to the uniforms they were wearing, well, I really couldn't say. They were just members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say as -- which army were these people part of? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: At the time, they were part of the army of the soldiers in the barracks in Benkovac. That's where they had been trained. That's the location they had been taken to. They'd been called to join that unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to tell me what army that unit pertained to, whether it was part of the JNA or some other army or some other force or you simply don't know?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, as has already been said, there were other men wearing JNA uniforms. Some even had the cockade caps that they were wearing. I remember someone with a beard, with fair hair who was wearing a cockade cap from the former war. They wore all sorts of things, but I don't know whether this is something that had been organised or something that was done purely as a provocative act. Among the troops there were such individuals too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm focused on these four people that escorted you to Knin. What were they wearing? Describe them as precisely as you can.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms like the regular JNA troops, the Yugoslav People's Army troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Where did they take you in Knin?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They took us to the south camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of facility was this thing you refer to as the south camp?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It's large complex. There was a heliport there used by helicopters. It was a fairly large complex. The troops had accommodation there. There were warehouses on the grounds behind the hills. There were vehicles and weapons. I don't know what sort of weapons they actually had because they were all being used in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You say the troops had accommodation there. Was this some kind of barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long were you held in these barracks? How long were you detained there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They detained us in the barracks until we had cleared everything. The -- the arrival of Pajo's helmets. That's what they called them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you give me an estimate in terms of days or months about how long you were held in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, they kept us there -- well, if I was there for six and a half months -- well, not even for five months. We were there for less than five months. Up until the day that these people arrived. We didn't have any pencils or papers or pens, so we couldn't keep a record of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. That's an approximation. What kind of room were you held in when you first arrived at these barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in the barracks, they first abused us when we got off the lorry that we had been transported in. They tied us up, threw us on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did they take you into any kind of room or where -- where did you spend the nights at the beginning there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They put us up against a wall. We had to kiss the wall and our fatherland and the King. We had to do that for about two hours for sure. And then afterwards they took us into a corridor, and then beat us there until about 1.00 or 12.00 and a little after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me. Okay. You say, "They put us up against a wall and we had to kiss the wall and our fatherland." Could you explain that a little bit more, what happened to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We had to take an oath for the King and the fatherland, the Serbian fatherland, call it what you will. They said we had to take an oath and kiss the wall in support of the King and the fatherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was anything else happening to you as you were told to kiss this wall and stand in front of the wall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If they weren't satisfied with our kisses, they insisted on us kissing the walls a little more intensively. The kisses were not very convincing. We had to make more expressive gestures. I was -- I feared for my teeth when they ordered us to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And then -- then they took you into a corridor where you were beaten some more. What happened after that? Did you go somewhere else after that corridor?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: After that, they took us to three small houses, houses that were used for special units. They took us into one of the small houses, the third one in the series when you go along the corridor, and we spent two days there. I apologise. We spent three days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How big was that house that you spent three days in?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's about three and a half by three. It wouldn't be four metres. Well, let's say it was four metres by four metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how many people were held in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there, no one was there, only we were there. Later on, they brought in an old man, Jero who was 80 years old. They also maltreated him. He had thrombosis of the leg. They brought him in and he stayed with us. He was the only other person there in addition to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about the other houses? After three days did you go into any of the other small houses?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Three days later, they moved us. There was Mate Sicic, people who had been there before. Mate Sicic a retired colonel, he brought his people from Puljani and the surrounding places. In fact, he tricked them to go to a meeting in Knin. He collected the people himself and took them to the prison in Knin. So there were about eight of them and us. Seventeen or 18 of us altogether in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how big was that room?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The size was the same. All three houses were of the same size.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What condition were the people in, in these rooms? Now I'm talking about first room you were in and then this other room. What condition were the people in there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: You mean in material terms what the condition was like? What exactly are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I mean their physical condition, their medical condition.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were young people, between 30 and 40 years of age, apart from Jero, the old man. He was about 70 years old and there was Mate Sicic, the colonel, the retired colonel. He was an elderly person. All the other people were younger people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about their health condition? How was their health?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, Jero was in a very poor condition. He was exhausted. His leg was falling apart. He had thrombosis. That's what we could call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like you to --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Then there were people who were in a state of delirium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, in a state of delirium?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: These people had remained without any alcohol, and that's probably why they were in a state of delirium. And they couldn't smoke, so they were in a crisis, in a state of delirium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where did you sleep while you were in these rooms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We slept on the floor. There was just one plank used to sleep on. There was nothing else there. And everyone else slept on concrete. And we were given one blanket each.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you given a blanket in those rooms at the beginning when you first arrived at this -- at these barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no. Not -- we were given a blanket when we arrived in that room, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where did you go when you had to use the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We had a 30-litre pail. That's what we used. A 30-litre bucket. And there was a blue coat that belonged to Petar Gurlica which we tore up into pieces and we used these pieces as toilet paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was the smell like in those rooms, in that second room in particular?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Those who were in a state of delirium would defecate in the middle of the room next to the door, and then we would have to clean this up. And then four people arrived, two men and two women, with cameras to photograph us. Then these two women ran away through the door. They couldn't support that. And then they shot some more film. They said they were from the Belgrade radio and television centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you provided with food and water in these barracks, in those rooms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: For a while it was terrible. You'd receive something and then the other person would receive something, but by that time you'd already eaten everything. There were no plates. In fact, there were plates but they didn't provide us with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did they provide you with water to drink?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not for the first three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And after the first three days, did you get sufficient water to drink?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Then they provided us -- they provided us with a limited amount of water for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have any water to wash yourselves with?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No, we never had water of that kind. We didn't even dream of having such water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How were you treated by the guards while you were held in these rooms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: How did they behave? Well, they beat us. While we were in the small houses they would beat us, and then there was a break, a short break, and then later whoever wanted to have a go at us would do so. Some would come back from the field who would be angry or unhappy, and then they'd beat whoever they felt like beating. They were always trying to find reasons to beat us. They'd say that we had pulled out the fingernails of their children, that we had done this, that we had done that. They'd think up stories as a pretext for beating and torturing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How often were you beaten? Was it every day or every week? How frequent was it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned when we left the houses and arrived in the sports hall, after a wall they occasionally beat individuals. And as far as I and the others are concerned, they would sometimes hit us but this wasn't fairly frequent. For a fairly long period of time they really didn't beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But before we get to the sports hall, how frequently in those rooms, how frequently were you and the others beaten in those rooms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: In those rooms they beat us severely. I couldn't stand up. So somebody could help me stand up. If I was lying down, I couldn't stand up. If I was sitting, I couldn't get up from the chair. There was a vet who was there for 15 days. He couldn't sleep, so he helped me. For 20 days I slept standing up. If I lied down, I couldn't stand up. Everything was wet on the ground. It would freeze. So it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know, you referred to a vet who was there for 15 days. Was that a prisoner or someone who worked in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No. He was brought -- he was brought in. He was in prison, but he was soon released because they needed him in the field. He was in their area, in the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Other than whatever help this vet could have provided you, did anyone -- did anyone receive medical care for the beatings or the other conditions that they had while they were in these rooms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No, no one received medical care. A little later I received some sort of elastic bandage when I was hit here. I have problems with my hand. But while I was imprisoned I didn't receive a single pill, nor did anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you be any more specific about who it was who was beating you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, the guards. I didn't know these people. I didn't know their first and last names. That was impossible. Later, I'd hear some of their names but that's something you forget. I've written down some of their names. I don't know if you have this on paper, but I have the names of some of the guards. They would beat us for a certain period of time and then they would give up. Some went into the field. Others remained there in the end. But I think there were only three of them who stayed on till the end, and these people were a little better than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what -- what force these people that beat you belonged to? Were they Yugoslav army? Were they paramilitaries? Were they someone else? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The people who remained, as I have already said, they no longer had the five-pointed stars. They had the JA insignia, Yugoslav army insignia, and the Serbian flag. That was the sort of insignia they had. I didn't see anything else. SAO Krajina, well this is something you could see on all of them. And then there was the JA insignia and the White Eagles, the Beli Orlovi insignia, but I didn't see anything else. As for the individuals who were wearing the cockade caps, et cetera, if Benkovac, well, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier you mentioned that at some point you were taken to the sports hall. When -- when did that happen? How long had you been in the rooms when you were taken to the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: That happened about and month, a month and a half later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how long did you spend in the sports hall, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We remained there until UNPROFOR arrived. We were transferred a few days before UNPROFOR took over the premises, because we had to clean the premises, put goods away in warehouses, load the coal from the railway station. We did this for a few days before Christmas. And when we had done all of this, I left. They called this prison Martic's prison. Only I went there and two others. The others were transferred to the old wing of the hospital and some people were up on the floor which was also part of the so-called Martic's prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We'll get to that but I want to ask you a few more questions about the sports hall. Are you able to estimate in terms of days or months or weeks about how long you were in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: For about three and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many people were held with you in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, 75 individuals was the minimum, but sometimes there were over 150 or 170 and sometimes almost 200 people. But people kept leaving, others kept arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions in the sports hall, where you slept, how you went to the toilet, these kind of things?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Occasionally they let us go to the toilet in the sports hall. They'd take us there in groups but we'd only have five minutes for the toilet. If we didn't have enough time, they'd send us back. We would also be beaten. Not everyone, but they would beat us severely. When it was necessary to urinate there was a barrel of -- 200-litre barrel that was next to the door and that's what we had to use to urinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who Ratko Mladic is?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Ratko Mladic yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came on two occasions to the sports hall. He arrived in a helicopter that landed at the heliport and then came to see us. That was in wintertime. He would always say that we should break through some sort of a windowpane. That was a kind of provocative sign. He says that meant we would spend the entire winter there. When he came the second time he said, "You still haven't broken the windowpane," and said, "While I'm here, you won't leave the prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything about Skabrnja at the times when you saw him at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He went from door-to-door and asked where everyone was from, and each person would say where he or she was from, and when he arrived where I was together with the others, he pointed to me and asked me where I was from. I said I was from Skabrnja. He didn't say anything. He just moved on. But before he asked me where I was from, he told others, "If you don't do what you are told -- what -- your fate will be the same as the fate of the inhabitants from Skabrnja." I assume he didn't know we were from Skabrnja or perhaps he did. But nevertheless, he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if my math is a little better this time, I think it's now time for the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have another three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps my watch is wrong, Your Honour. I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go by this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. It's a little hard -- I see. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, how long were you held -- no. Sorry, I already asked you that. Where did you go when you left the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I went away for ten days. Then there was Martic's prison. I was put up there. Blaskic's son and father were exchanged. This was organised through an officer who I think had retired. His daughter was a daughter in Novi Grad. They had a summer house, and they probably got him out because they were friends. Through the old hospital they were released but me, Lacic and three others who went to work on bars for the prison, this was for the old hospital. I and Lacic went there for about ten days. Tomislav Lacic. His wife also worked with doctor, dentist. She was a sort of medical orderly. We made the bars. There were guards with us in this locksmith's shop. Once we had done this they returned us. And when these people left for the exchange, when the Blaskic's were exchanged, I was returned to my people in the cellar. In the second wing --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, let me interrupt you. We're going to have to take this one step at a time. When you first left the barracks to come to this place that you call Martic's prison, tell me how that happened. Why did you go to the place you call Martic's prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was designed to be a nine-men group to make these bars. There was this little guardhouse, we had to make bars for the gym and another place. We didn't know the assignment in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where was this place that you're referring to as Martic's prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It's not that I called it Martic's prison. Everybody called it Martic's prison. That's how it was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: In the old hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say you went there with some other people. And where were you detained when you went to Martic's prison in the old hospital?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: We were locked up in what they called room number 1. There were two hallways forking near that room. One went left, and the other went straight ahead and down to the basement. These hallways crossed the entire building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we'll have to continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We will come back at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is sorry about the delay. It was due to circumstances beyond our control. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I resume the examination, there are just two brief points I'd like to raise. The first one is simply that we provided a translation of the supplementary information sheet for this witness. The Defence mentioned earlier at that there was no translation, so we just provided that at the break. The second issue regards the schedule, Your Honour. I've spoken with the Defence, and we think we've agreed on a position, and so I'm proposing to see if it's acceptable to the Trial Chamber. What we would suggest is that I would finish the direct examination of Mr. Brkic today, which I think will take me about another whatever an hour. At that point, we would stop with his testimony and tomorrow have the testimony of the next witness, Josip Josipovic. That is one of the witnesses that came here and had to be home and now he's back again. Now he has had to take the last days of his annual leave and we really want to finish him this week. We think if we can do that tomorrow he'll finish easily in one day and we can send him home and then Defence counsel would have some more time to consider their cross-examination. Mr. Brkic could be cross-examined on Friday. I think it will finish. And those were the only two witnesses who would be prepared to testify this week anyhow. So I think that satisfies the Defence and the Prosecution, but we would like to know if it's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's exactly as the Prosecutor has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event then, that will be the procedure followed. I'm not quite sure whether we'll finish with this witness on Friday given the fact that I've already indicated we're going to be having a short day on Friday and the number of questions I think might arise from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. Nevertheless, I think this is the best scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, just as we left off you were telling us about how you had gone with some other men to Martic's prison. Please describe the room in which you were held in Martic's prison when you first arrived there.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was a room they called room number 1. That's all I know about it. It was small, just enough to hold a bed, and the rest of the space was free. Maybe two and a half by two and a half metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many men were held in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Nine of us there were bunkbeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How were you treated, the nine of you, in that room?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The nine of us in that room were treated all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if there were other people being detained in other rooms of this place, Martic's prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The same day when we were brought to that prison, to that room, another group of about 15, 16 people were brought just a few minutes later. I didn't count them. I'm just saying roughly. They were from somewhere between Grahovo and Livno. Some operation had been carried out there, and those people were brought into the prison. They remained closer to the entrance door, whereas our room was closer to the toilets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those people while they were there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: When we were sent to that room number 1 and locked up, those people remained still outside, and we were no longer able to see them. That evening, we had yet another group that was brought in after them, maybe an hour later, about the same number of people, which we found out later when we were allowed to go outside to work. That was in the afternoon. And then some sort of fight broke -- sorry. Then they started beating that last group of people that were brought in, and it was a harrowing scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Describe the scene.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It happened near room number 1. I told you there's a fork of hallways. It's the L portion of that hallway. And it went on and on and day after day after lunch, and especially after dinner. And it would go on until 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How were these people beaten?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were beaten with anything they could lay their hands on. Once when I was allowed to go out to the toilet, I saw two men beating somebody with two plastic bags filled with sand. Large, one-litre plastic bags. And the man had his hands tied in the back. They probably kicked him as well. They had weapons. They could have used rifle butts. That's just one thing that I saw. The rest I was unable to see. I just heard moaning, cries, screams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who participated in the beating? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I cannot know that. All I know is that people came across the fence. Some people who worked outside mixing mortar for construction told us through the window about this. They were some people who just beat others for the pleasure of it. They were not policemen or anything. They just enjoyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about -- excuse me. What about the people that you saw doing some beating? Were they wearing uniforms, or how were they dressed? The ones that you saw yourself.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms. There were some among them whom I knew from Smiljanic. Some of them wore blue regular official uniforms, those ones that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the ones who wore the blue uniforms, do you know what group or what force they were a part of?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The Martic's -- the Martic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you see Martic's police on any other occasions in this prison in the hospital, Martic's prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Those two that I knew really well, the Grahovac brothers from Smiljcici were there all the time. They would even come to see me when we were transferred to the basement. They would talk to me through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How do you know that the Grahovac brothers were members of Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: How could I not know? They were wearing uniforms of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of this -- this prison in the hospital, the part where you were -- you've just been describing?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I could not tell you that, because I don't know exactly who was in charge. I just knew some people who were inside, and I knew some of the people in uniform. There was one man, Djuro, from somewhere in Plavno. He was a very dangerous man. And another one was called Momo, Momir Cupac. He talked to me a lot about many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what force or what group Djuro and Momir belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: They were also members of Martic -- Martic's Police, as far as I could understand from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long were you held in this small room in Martic's prison? How many days?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: All in all 12 days. When we finished making the bars and when they were mounted on the windows, which I helped do. They later put bars on another two windows without me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where did you go after those 12 days?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to join the people who had been with me before in the south camp. They were placed in one of the wings of the hospital in its ground level. That's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that a different part of the same hospital where you were when you were in Martic's prison?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that window is linked to that subterranean level by a staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And who controlled this part of the hospital where you were now?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, it belonged to the army. By that time it had already turned into JA, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I remained there until I was released to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you estimate how long that was in terms of weeks or months or days?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: A little over a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And describe for us the conditions there during that month. How were the conditions in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, the rooms were again very, very small. If two men lie down, for instance I and another man, my feet reached to his armpits and vice versa. We couldn't lie one next to the other. We had to lie in opposite directions so as to fit together, so to speak. But the rooms next to us were slightly bigger. It was not that bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you physically mistreated in any way while you were in this part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Right. They abused us even more and started beating us even more frequently and more severely once it became known that we would be exchanged. Like every 20 minutes or so. Some people say that there were even attempts to rape men. I don't really know if that happened or not, but some people said it happened in the next room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was participating in the beating in this part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: The most violent of all was this Djuro. I heard later that he was killed during Operation Storm, but he was among the most violent. They dragged me several times into the hallway like they did others, too, but I'm now talking about myself. Every time there would be four or five of them beating you on the back, and you turn your back and you try to handle it as long as you can and then you can't do it any more and you turn over on your stomach and they start beating you on the belly. And all that happened to others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who occupied the floor or the floors above where you were being held in that part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: There was the duty guards' room only. Somebody had to go upstairs to clean, and I went several times to clean. Nobody wanted to go. This small man, Djuro, sat there, the commander, and some of the rooms were filled with prisoners. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember what day you were exchanged when you were released from detention?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: It was in May, on the day of statehood or day of independence. I think it's the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkic, for your patience getting through that. You've been describing your detention after you were captured in Skabrnja. I'd like to show you a document. It's 65 ter number 670. The ERN is 04006313 to 6316. My preference would be to have it pulled up on e-court and also to give a hard copy to the witness, please. Mr. Brkic, I'd like you to take a moment and just through that list, please. You don't need to read it out loud, just look at it for a moment. Mr. Brkic, do you see your own name near the bottom of the first page there? Which is page 4 in the English version. It's actually near the top of page 4 in the English. Are you able to find your name, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's closer to the bottom, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Brkic, it says there, "Member of the ZNG." Were you a member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the other names on this list as being the names of people who were detained with you in Knin?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I know Anto Elkaz and lots of young men from Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just a look through the entire document, and you don't have to go name by name, but do you recognise some of the names here as people who were detained with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mato Civcic, Anto Elkaz, and some other people who were in other rooms and whom I was unable to see, some people who were there before me and left before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just before your own name, you can see the names of Petar Gurlica --

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were those people also in detention in Knin?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this receive a number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an objection, Your Honour. On this document there is no heading nor seal nor reference number nor the signature of the person who made the list. We don't even know the title of that person. To what extent -- we don't even have a witness's answer to the provenance of this document. Actually, the witness tried to say today that he saw some people on the list at the prison, but I can't understand want kind of document we are looking at, where it comes from, who made it. We have lots of indications here like who is holding the person, the date of capture and other details, but the document itself is completely invalid, incomplete. It's difficult even to discern where it comes from, where it originates, and what it means. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Milovancevic forces me to revisit this issue. In paragraph 6 of the guidelines on the standards governing the admission of evidence adopted by Your Honours, it says, "When objection are raised on the grounds of authenticity or reliability, this Trial Chamber will follow the practice of this Tribunal, namely to admit documents and video recordings and then decide on the weight to be given to them within the context of the Trial Record as a whole." In paragraph 5 it specifically says: "The fact that a document is unsigned or unstamped does not a priori render it void of authenticity. Authenticity and proof of authorship will assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces in the framework of the free evaluation of evidence." This evidence under Rule 89(C) is relevant. It has probative value. The witness has testified that his own name is accurately recorded there and the names of other prisoners that he knew -- personally knows were in detention. Your Honour, I see no grounds for excluding this document. I think any question as to its provenance or authenticity should go to weight. That's the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see this document has got an ERN number. Was it given to the Defence with the OTP documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's on our 65 ter exhibit list. It was given to the Defence some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any reply, Mr. Milovancevic? Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this document is on the 65 ter list. I couldn't say for certain for the following reason: When we received the lists of this kind from the Prosecution on each of the lists in one of the vertical columns there is a section that concerns when the individual was released and on the basis of whose decision. So this could be a document that might be in accord with other documents provided to us by the Prosecution, but we haven't such a case here. Perhaps something was left out when this document was transcribed. I don't know what the situation is. When my learned colleague from the Prosecution quotes the Rules that are in force, well, that is not in dispute, but we have no information concerning the provenance of this document and, likewise, the witness was not able to tell us the origin of this document, and the Prosecutor couldn't tell us either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are quite a number of documents that have been given to the Defence in advance whose origin witnesses could not talk to. The ruling of the Chamber is that the document will be admitted into evidence. May it be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance again of the court officer and the usher, I'd like to show the witness another document. It's 65 ter number 2388, and the ERN is 04192653 to 2664. And again, if I could hand the witness a hard copy I think it would make it easier for him to flip through. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, again take a few moments to look over this. It's another list of names. And when you get to it, tell me if you see your own name at 51 on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps if the e-court could be forwarded a couple of pages until we arrive. On the English version it appears on the bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour. The witness is looking at the B/C/S version, the original, and there's an English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a B/C/S version of the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness was looking at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there at some stage the possibility of the Chamber looking at the B/C/S version or if it could be put on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely possible. With the current document I think the B/C/S is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you see your own name there at number 51?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is the -- and then it says "Skabrnja, 19 November 91." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that correct that you began your detention in Knin on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: That's when I arrived in Knin. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Again, I'd like you to just look through this list - take a couple moments if you need to - and tell me if you're able to say whether any of the other people named here were also detained in Knin.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you see any names specifically that you remember being there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Drago Agic. Sunkovci. I can remember this person called Vlado. I know Curko. He wasn't with me. I think he came afterwards or perhaps he arrived there before. Josip Aralica. He did the same sort of work that I did later on. Atelj Ivan. Miraz was there. And then from backwards onwards almost all of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this also receive a number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, and may it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I'm done now asking about your detention, and I want to move to another topic, so you can put that document to the side. When was the first time you were able to return to Skabrnja after your detention, after you were released and exchanged?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I returned after the Storm operation, but I wasn't in a hurry then. I was still in uniform, and I was in Sipurine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What did you find when you returned to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: I found everything that's depicted in the photographs. Everything had been destroyed. The houses had been destroyed. Burnt down. My house had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You refer to some photographs. Let me show you Exhibit 272. And again, I'll hand the witness hand copies, but if it could be brought up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I believed last time you asked if we have copies for the Bench, so brought copies of this photo booklet for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you remember me showing you those photographs earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, just continue to look through them. Take a few moments, and when you're done please tell me if these accurately reflect the way Skabrnja looked upon your return in 1995.

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This does reflect the situation in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can put those photos aside now. I'm going to be done with my questions, just one last topic. You've described to us what you went through in detention in Knin. Could you now tell us what kind of physical effects you suffered from your detention even after you were released? Do you have any physical effects from that time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I still do. When I returned, I was a different man. I -- in terms of my physical appearance, et cetera. I'm still receiving medical treatment, but only temporarily. This is to help me to recover, so to speak. In prison, I probably got hepatitis B. I'm now immune. I went to check this up somewhere. I was -- I received food poisoning on two occasions. Hepatitis B is something you get through the blood, direct through the blood. I have a bruised back, and my stomach split in this way when I was beaten up. We returned to our homes black and blue once all of this was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, thank you very much for answering all my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you agree that we are postponing the cross-examination by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that finishes us for the day then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, court adjourned to tomorrow at 2.00 in this Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could perhaps explain to the witness that he's returning on Friday so he understand the timing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, although we're coming back to court tomorrow, you don't have to come tomorrow. You may -- you should only come back on Friday, the 7th, and be here at about half past nine at the very latest. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of April, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
